Lemon sole (Microstomus kitt) hatch from pelagic eggs with a diameter of approximately 1.29 mm, a modest size that constrains the initial mass of the resulting prolarvae. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae carry an endogenous nutritional supply, and the newly emerged individuals exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0011 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0011 grams]. This minute starting mass is typical of many flatfishes that produce numerous pelagic offspring. The time required for embryonic development to reach the hatching stage is tightly linked to ambient temperature; for this species, eggs incubated at 15.3 °C [T = 15.3 °C] will hatch after about 5.5 days [ab = about 5.5 days], a relatively short incubation period that reflects the elevated metabolic rates sustained under such warm conditions. The small size of the hatchling and the rapid pace of early ontogeny represent a life-history strategy that prioritizes numerical output over per-offspring investment, a pattern frequently observed in marine teleosts that broadcast spawn in the water column.

As Lemon sole larvae undergo the exotrophic transition and begin actively feeding on planktonic prey, somatic growth proceeds steadily. The duration of the larval phase is influenced by temperature, and metamorphosis ultimately leads to a benthic juvenile stage. During this period of rapid mass increase, the fish accumulate the structural tissues that will determine their eventual adult dimensions. Field surveys and length-frequency analyses indicate that the maximum total length attainable by this species is 65 cm [Li = 65 cm], which represents the ultimate size achieved by the largest individuals in the population. This asymptotic length is consistent with the values reported for other pleuronectid flatfishes inhabiting the northeast Atlantic continental shelf. The onset of reproductive maturity, however, occurs well before this maximum size is reached. Data collected from commercial catches and research trawl surveys suggest that females first attain sexual maturity when they reach a total length at puberty of 31.5 cm [Lp = 31.5 cm], a size that corresponds to roughly half the ultimate length. This length-based threshold for maturity is a key demographic parameter used in stock assessment models.

The relationship between length and body mass in Lemon sole follows a standard cubic growth pattern, allowing researchers to derive weight at key life-history transitions from length measurements. Applying this allometric relationship, the wet weight at puberty for a female measuring 31.5 cm is estimated to be 389 grams [Wwp = 389 grams], representing the typical body mass at which gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis are first initiated. This pubertal mass is considerably less than the ultimate female wet weight, which approaches 3.5 kilograms [Wwi = 3.5 kilograms] under favorable conditions. The substantial difference between these two weight milestones reflects a prolonged period of somatic growth that continues for several years after the onset of sexual maturity. Field observations indicate that most females do not reach their maximum size until well into their reproductive lifespan, with growth rates gradually decelerating as they approach the asymptotic length. This pattern of indeterminate growth is typical among flatfishes and has important implications for estimating lifetime fecundity and reproductive output in exploited populations.

Reproductive investment in Lemon sole is characterized by a high fecundity that is modulated by both body size and ambient temperature. During the spawning season, which occurs in spring and early summer, individual females produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs. Fecundity per reproductive event is substantial, with well-fed, large females depositing approximately 1,836 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,836 eggs per spawning event]. The frequency of these spawning events is also relatively high; under the thermal conditions typical of the species' spawning grounds, females are capable of producing approximately one spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per day] when maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This combination of high batch fecundity and near-daily spawning frequency generates a total daily reproductive output that is among the highest documented for northeast Atlantic flatfishes of comparable body size. The energetic costs of sustaining such a high rate of egg production are substantial and are likely met by intensive feeding during the pre-spawning period, when females accumulate the lipid reserves necessary for vitellogenesis.

Otolith ageing studies of wild-caught specimens have been instrumental in determining the maximum lifespan of Lemon sole. The oldest individuals documented in the northeast Atlantic have been recorded at 23 years [am = 23 years], a longevity that places this species among the longer-lived members of the Pleuronectidae at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This lifespan is realized under the typical thermal regime of their continental shelf habitat, where bottom water temperatures average 10 °C [T = 10 °C] throughout much of the year. Such an extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances high annual fecundity against a relatively protracted period of growth and maturation. The combination of a late age at maturity, substantial ultimate body size, and a long reproductive window allows individual females to produce millions of eggs over the course of their lives, contributing significantly to population resilience. Comparative analyses with congeneric species such as Microstomus pacificus suggest that the maximum size and longevity of Lemon sole are attuned to the seasonal productivity patterns of its temperate habitat.
